Corruption-Robust Sparse Linear Contextual Bandits with Knapsack Constraints

Yige Wang†,Hanyang Li†,Yiming Zong†\text{Yige Wang}^{\dagger},\text{Hanyang Li}^{\dagger},\text{Yiming Zong}^{\dagger}    Wanteng Ma‡⁣∗\text{Wanteng Ma}^{{\ddagger}*}    Jiashuo Jiang†⁣∗\text{Jiashuo Jiang}^{{\dagger}*}
Abstract

We study sparse linear contextual bandits with knapsack constraints under joint reward and consumption corruption. Consumption corruption creates a challenge beyond corrupted rewards: it affects not only statistical estimates, but also the recorded budget, resource prices, and stopping decisions that govern future allocation. We develop Robust Optimistic Primal–Dual (ROPD), an estimator-modular framework that combines corruption-aware confidence widths with online resource prices and a budget-safety rule. With concrete sparse implementation, ROPD achieves regret against a clean population-LP benchmark of O~​(T2/3+Γ​T1/3)\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3}+\Gamma T^{1/3}) under forced exploration and population-design coverage, and O~​(T+Γ)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}+\Gamma) under on-policy realized-design coverage, for a supplied valid corruption bound Γ\Gamma under the stated proportional-budget scaling and fixed model/design parameters. When the corruption level is unknown, Shared-Grid adapts confidence radii around common point estimates fitted to a single realized history, incurring explicit initialization and master-comparison costs; its sharper on-policy guarantee additionally requires recommendation coverage. Both methods preserve observed budgets on every realization and bound clean resource violation by cumulative consumption corruption. These results connect corruption-robust sparse estimation with resource accounting, pricing, and stopping in high-dimensional online allocation.

keywords
Contextual Bandits with Knapsacks; Sparse Linear Bandits; Adversarial Corruption; Online Resource Allocation; Primal–Dual Learning

1 Introduction

Contextual bandits with knapsack constraints (CBwK) couple learning with resource allocation: after observing a context, a learner chooses an action whose reward must be learned while its consumption depletes finite budgets (badanidiyuru2018bandits, agrawal2016linear, agrawal2016efficient). In high-dimensional applications, only a small subset of features may govern reward and consumption, motivating sparse action-specific models (bastani2020online, hao2020high, ma2023high).

Corruption of consumption feedback creates a difficulty beyond corrupted rewards. A corrupted reward changes what the learner infers about an action, whereas corrupted consumption also changes the state used to allocate future resources—consumption estimate, recorded budget, resource prices, and potentially stopping time. For example, an advertisement that is truly expensive but repeatedly recorded as inexpensive can be favored while the observed budget account still appears feasible.

A robust estimator alone therefore does not resolve the allocation problem. The analysis must control how corrupted observations affect later predictions, relate observed consumption to the latent clean resource use, and account for reward lost when corrupted resource information changes stopping. In the sparse setting, these guarantees also depend on whether the contexts actually collected for each action are informative. When the corruption level is unknown, candidates calibrated to different levels may recommend different actions even though feedback is observed only for the actions that are actually played.

We address these issues with Robust Optimistic Primal–Dual (ROPD), which combines corruption-aware prediction widths with online resource prices and a budget-safety rule. The allocation analysis is estimator-modular: it uses only pointwise confidence and cumulative uncertainty along the recommended actions. Norm-constrained Lasso provides one concrete sparse implementation. We study both forced exploration and on-policy learning, and for unknown corruption introduce Shared-Grid, which compares confidence calibrations around common point estimates fitted to one realized history.

1.1 Main Contributions

1. Joint statistical and resource effects of corruption. We measure joint reward–consumption corruption through the priced budget CZC_{Z} and separate its two roles: contaminated samples affect future prediction, while corrupted consumption directly changes resource accounting, price updates, and stopping. This decomposition yields regret guarantees together with exact observed-budget feasibility and an explicit bound on clean resource violation.

2. Estimator-modular robust allocation with two data routes. Given a valid bound Γ≥CZ\Gamma\geq C_{Z}, ROPD combines optimistic predictions with online resource prices. Its allocation theorem requires only pointwise confidence and cumulative recommendation-width control; norm-constrained Lasso is one concrete implementation. Forced exploration under population design gives the O~​(T2/3)\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3}) corruption-free regime, while realized on-policy design gives O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}) under the conditions summarized in Table 1.

3. Adaptation to unknown corruption on shared data. Shared-Grid compares corruption calibrations around common point estimates fitted to the single realized history, rather than analyzing candidates on counterfactual estimator histories. Its guarantee retains initialization and master-comparison costs explicitly; the sharper on-policy result additionally requires coverage of candidate recommendations by realized plays.

Relation to closest work. Clean high-dimensional CBwK already combines sparse estimation with primal–dual resource control (ma2023high), while corruption-robust linear and contextual bandits primarily address corrupted reward feedback without knapsack state (he2022nearly, liu2024corruption). Thus the new difficulty here is not sparse estimation or dual pricing in isolation: corrupted consumption simultaneously affects prediction, resource-price path, recorded budget, and stopping. We analyze these effects against a clean population-LP benchmark and, when the corruption level is unknown, adapt on a single realized estimator history. Section 1.2 gives the broader comparison.

1.2 Related Work

Contextual bandits with knapsacks and high-dimensional allocation. The CBwK framework joins bandit learning with finite resource constraints (badanidiyuru2018bandits). agrawal2016linear study the closest clean linear contextual model: expected rewards and resource consumptions are linear in observed features, and confidence sets are combined with online resource prices to control the knapsacks. agrawal2016efficient develop a more general oracle-based contextual framework, and primal–dual ideas also connect this literature to online packing and dynamic resource allocation (agrawal2014bandits, devanur2009adwords, agrawal2014dynamic). Our known-corruption method keeps the basic confidence-plus-price structure, but the feedback used by the estimator, the dual update, and the stopping rule can now differ from the clean process used by the benchmark. Our analysis accounts for the difference between clean and observed consumption in the price updates and the reward lost after stopping. Adversarial and non-stationary BwK study changing reward and consumption environments (immorlica2022adversarial, liu2022non), while instance-dependent BwK analyses go beyond worst-case guarantees under clean feedback (sankararaman2021bandits). Our model instead keeps a latent uncorrupted linear contextual model with i.i.d. contexts and studies corrupted observations of that process, so the goal is to recover performance against a clean population-LP benchmark.

Sparse contextual bandits and clean high-dimensional CBwK. Sparse contextual bandit methods use regularization, forced sampling, Thompson sampling, or hard thresholding so regret depends on a small relevant support (bastani2020online, hao2020high, ren2024dynamic, chakraborty2023thompson). The closest paper to our sparse allocation setting is ma2023high, which combines an online hard-thresholding estimator with a primal–dual CBwK method and obtains logarithmic dependence on the ambient feature dimension under clean feedback. Their sharper clean regime and our zero-corruption on-policy result both have O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}) horizon dependence, with different action, sparsity, curvature, norm, and resource-price factors. This comparison concerns the horizon exponent, not identical dimension dependence. Our setting adds corrupted reward and consumption observations, a direct resource-accounting term, a sequential charge for the later effect of corrupted action-specific samples, and adaptation when the corruption level is unknown. The retained-design RSC condition in our sharper result plays the familiar statistical role of ensuring that action-specific data identify sparse parameters. The additional Shared-Grid recommendation-coverage condition is different: it controls how often candidate recommendations are supported by realized plays.

Corruption-robust bandits. Corruption-robust bandit work first showed how regret can degrade with an adversarial corruption budget in stochastic multi-armed bandits (lykouris2018stochastic, gupta2019better). Later work studies linear and contextual models. ding2022robust allow attacked rewards and contexts without requiring the attack budget. For a known played-action reward-corruption budget CC, he2022nearly obtain O~​(d​T+d​C)\widetilde{O}(d\sqrt{T}+dC) and also study adaptation without a supplied bound. For fixed-parameter linear bandits, liu2024corruption distinguish CC from the worst-action budget C∞C_{\infty} and establish O~​(d​T+min⁡{d​C,d​C∞})\widetilde{O}(d\sqrt{T}+\min\{dC,\sqrt{d}\,C_{\infty}\}) with matching lower bounds under the corresponding corruption information. These results concern reward corruption without knapsack constraints and do not by themselves establish optimal dependence on our joint reward–consumption budget. Other work studies linear optimization, Lipschitz bandits, generalized linear models, and explicit poisoning attacks (li2019stochastic, kang2023robust, yu2025corruption, liu2019data). These papers develop robust confidence sets, weighting, elimination, and attack-adaptive exploration for bandit objectives centered on prediction and action selection. Our setting adds a resource signal that changes both statistical estimates and the state of the allocation system. The ZZ-scaled budget measures corruption in the action score, and the proof also controls observed budget account, dual-price path, and stopping time.

Robust sparse estimation and sequential prediction. Robust sparse regression studies parameter recovery when some responses or samples are corrupted (chen2013robust, bhatia2015robust, balakrishnan2017computationally, diakonikolas2019outlier, prasad2020robust, liu2020high). Restricted-eigenvalue and sparse covariance conditions explain when high-dimensional parameters can be identified (bickel2009simultaneous, raskutti2010restricted, negahban2012unified, wainwright2019high, buhlmann2011statistics). These tools provide the statistical base of our estimator module, while an online allocation proof additionally requires the sum of reward and consumption widths along an adaptive action path. We prove this sequential bound by matching estimator sample set to its coverage event and by charging each corrupted observation through the later inverse action counts in which it still appears. Our concrete analysis uses norm-constrained Lasso with candidate-independent regularization. An enlarged-cone argument and an RSC tolerance yield explicit corruption-aware confidence, with a norm bound handling large corruption. The resulting allocation theorems transfer to any sparse estimator that supplies the same predictable pointwise and cumulative-width guarantees.

Unknown corruption and bandit model selection. Corralling and model-selection methods combine candidates or policy classes under partial feedback (agarwal2017corralling, foster2019model, pacchiano2020regret, pacchiano2022best, cutkosky2021dynamic, krishnamurthy2021optimal, ghosh2021model). agarwal2017corralling show that a master must avoid starving a candidate of feedback. foster2019model adapt to an unknown contextual model class, and pacchiano2022best combine model selection with guarantees for fixed-mean and adversarial rewards. Model selection has also been used for corruption-robust reinforcement learning (wei2022model). Unknown corruption in sparse CBwK adds a data-design problem. Two independently updated corruption candidates would choose different actions and would need different action-specific context histories, so the confidence set of an inactive candidate can depend on data that the learner never collected. The shared-estimator grid avoids reliance on these unobserved histories: every candidate uses the same realized point estimate, and the master compares only their current recommendations. The remaining candidate-coverage condition in the exploration-free result states when these recommendations receive enough realized plays for their shared confidence widths to be summed.

Our paper combines primal–dual resource control, corruption-robust learning, and sparse action-specific estimation in a setting where resource-consumption feedback is itself corrupted. This requires a relation between clean and observed resource use, stopping control through resource prices, sequential tracking of corrupted retained samples, and shared-estimator adaptation on one realized design.

2 Model, Feedback, and Benchmark

2.1 Interaction and Feedback

The learner interacts with the environment for TT rounds with mm resource budgets, B=(B1,…,Bm)⊤B=(B_{1},\ldots,B_{m})^{\top}, with Bi>0B_{i}>0 for every resource i∈[m]={1,…,m}i\in[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}. At round tt, it observes a context xt∈ℝdx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, a vector of features available before choosing an action. It then selects an action ata_{t} from KK alternatives, indexed by 𝒜=[K]={1,…,K}\mathcal{A}=[K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}, or chooses the null action 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null}, which gives zero reward and uses no resources. We write 𝒜0=𝒜∪{𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕}\mathcal{A}_{0}=\mathcal{A}\cup\{\mathtt{null}\} for the full action set and call the actions in 𝒜\mathcal{A} non-null actions. The learner receives reward and consumption feedback only for the action it selects; this feedback may be corrupted.

Clean outcomes and observed feedback. We distinguish three quantities: the expected outcome before corruption, its noisy realization, and the feedback observed after corruption. We use clean to mean before adversarial corruption, not without stochastic noise. For action aa and context xx, let r0​(a,x)r^{0}(a,x) be the clean expected reward and bi0​(a,x)b_{i}^{0}(a,x) the clean expected consumption of resource ii. These clean conditional means are linear in the context, with unknown coefficient vectors μa⋆,wa,i⋆∈ℝd\mu_{a}^{\star},w_{a,i}^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:

r0​(a,x)=⟨μa⋆,x⟩,bi0​(a,x)=⟨wa,i⋆,x⟩,i∈[m].r^{0}(a,x)=\left\langle\mu_{a}^{\star},x\right\rangle,\quad b_{i}^{0}(a,x)=\left\langle w_{a,i}^{\star},x\right\rangle,\quad i\in[m]. (1)

Write b0​(a,x)=(b10​(a,x),…,bm0​(a,x))⊤b^{0}(a,x)=(b_{1}^{0}(a,x),\ldots,b_{m}^{0}(a,x))^{\top} for the consumption-mean vector.

The clean realizations rtcl​(a)r_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a) and bt,icl​(a)b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a) equal these means plus ordinary stochastic noise, specified in Assumption 2.1 below. The adversary adds raw perturbations ξtr​(a)\xi_{t}^{r}(a) and ξt,ib​(a)\xi_{t,i}^{b}(a) to these realizations. The resulting feedback is clipped to [0,1][0,1]:

rt(a)=clip(rtcl(a)+ξtr(a),0,1),bt,i(a)=clip(bt,icl(a)+ξt,ib(a),0,1),\displaystyle r_{t}(a)=\clip(r_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a)+\xi_{t}^{r}(a),0,1),\quad b_{t,i}(a)=\clip(b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a)+\xi_{t,i}^{b}(a),0,1),

where clip⁡(z,0,1)=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,z}}\clip(z,0,1)=\min\{1,\max\{0,z\}\} truncates values outside this interval. The actual changes after clipping, rather than the raw perturbations, enter our corruption measures:

ctr​(a)=rt​(a)−rtcl​(a),ct,ib​(a)=bt,i​(a)−bt,icl​(a).c_{t}^{r}(a)=r_{t}(a)-r_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a),\quad c_{t,i}^{b}(a)=b_{t,i}(a)-b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a). (2)

The vectors btcl​(a)b_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a), bt​(a)b_{t}(a), and ctb​(a)c_{t}^{b}(a) collect the corresponding mm resource coordinates. Because both clean and observed outcomes lie in [0,1][0,1], |ctr​(a)|≤1|c_{t}^{r}(a)|\leq 1 and ‖ctb​(a)‖∞≤1\|c_{t}^{b}(a)\|_{\infty}\leq 1, where ‖v‖∞\|v\|_{\infty} is the largest absolute coordinate of vv. For the null action, all clean outcomes, observed outcomes, and corruption terms are zero.

These variables describe each action’s potential outcomes: the outcomes it would produce if selected. They are defined for all actions to permit comparisons, but only rt​(at)r_{t}(a_{t}) and bt​(at)b_{t}(a_{t}) are observed (Table 2). The adversary changes clean realizations, not their underlying means, and its raw perturbations have no probability model. Their total effect is measured by the corruption budget in Section 2.2. Clipping bounds feedback; it does not identify corrupted observations.

Information and within-round timing. For analysis, let ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} be the full history before round tt: all earlier contexts, actions, clean potential outcomes, corruption, and learner randomization. The learner’s own history contains earlier contexts, selected actions, observed feedback, and its past randomization, but not latent clean outcomes or corruption. Its decisions use only this observed history, the current context, and fresh independent randomness.

Before observing xtx_{t}, the learner applies the budget-safety check in Section 2.3. A round is active if this check passes; otherwise, it selects 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null} from that round onward. On an active round: (i) the learner observes xtx_{t}; (ii) conditional on ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} and xtx_{t}, the environment generates the clean potential outcomes and fixes the corruption for every action; (iii) the learner draws ata_{t} using fresh randomness that, conditional on ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} and xtx_{t}, is independent of these potential outcomes and corruption, and observes only rt​(at)r_{t}(a_{t}) and bt​(at)b_{t}(a_{t}); (iv) the learner records the observed resource use and updates its estimates and other algorithm variables.

Thus, corruption is non-anticipating: it may depend on ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, the current context, and the generated clean potential outcomes, but not on the learner’s fresh round-tt random seed. A sample is retained when it is used to fit the estimates in Section 3.1. Both the action and the sample’s eligibility for retention are determined before the current feedback is revealed.

    Contexts. Given ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, xtx_{t} has distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} and satisfies ‖xt‖2≤1\|x_{t}\|_{2}\leq 1.

  2. (ii)

    Clean outcomes. For every action and resource, rtcl​(a)=r0​(a,xt)+ηtr​(a)r_{t}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a)=r^{0}(a,x_{t})+\eta_{t}^{r}(a) and bt,icl​(a)=bi0​(a,xt)+ηt,ib​(a)b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a)=b_{i}^{0}(a,x_{t})+\eta_{t,i}^{b}(a), where 𝔼[ηtr(a)∣ℱt−1,xt]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta_{t}^{r}(a)\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},x_{t}]=0 and 𝔼[ηt,ib(a)∣ℱt−1,xt]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta_{t,i}^{b}(a)\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},x_{t}]=0. The reward noise ηtr\eta_{t}^{r} and consumption noise ηt,ib\eta_{t,i}^{b} are conditionally sub-Gaussian with parameters at most σr\sigma_{r} and σb\sigma_{b}, respectively. Clean rewards and every clean consumption coordinate lie in [0,1][0,1].

Clean noise has mean zero given the full history and current context, and the sub-Gaussian parameters control its tail fluctuations. With the timing above, this supports concentration of retained clean-noise sums and unbiased importance-weighted comparisons in the unknown-corruption analysis. 2.2 Benchmark, Resource Prices, and Effective Corruption

Clean benchmark and regret. We evaluate the learner using clean rewards rather than corrupted feedback. The benchmark is a population linear program (LP) based on the context distribution and clean conditional means. Let y⁡(a∣x)y(a\mid x) be the probability of choosing non-null action aa given context xx, with remaining probability assigned to 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null}. This rule can depend on the context but is the same across rounds. Writing 𝔼x\mathbb{E}_{x} for expectation over x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}, the LP maximizes expected reward subject to expected resource budgets:

VUB:=maxy\displaystyle V^{\mathrm{UB}}:=\max_{y} T​𝔼x​[∑a∈𝒜r0​(a,x)​y​(a∣x)]\displaystyle T\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}r^{0}(a,x)y(a\mid x)\right] (3)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} T𝔼x[∑a∈𝒜bi0(a,x)y(a∣x)]≤Bi,i∈[m],\displaystyle T\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}b_{i}^{0}(a,x)y(a\mid x)\right]\leq B_{i},\quad i\in[m],
y(a∣x)≥0,∑a∈𝒜y(a∣x)≤1,∀x.\displaystyle y(a\mid x)\geq 0,\quad\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}y(a\mid x)\leq 1,\quad\forall x.

Under the i.i.d. model, this value upper-bounds the clean expected reward attainable under the population resource constraints (agrawal2016linear, agrawal2016efficient). For the analysis, fix a measurable optimizer y⋆y^{\star} before interaction. The learner does not know or solve this LP. Its clean expected regret is

Reg⁡(T):=VUB−𝔼⁡[∑t=1Tr0​(at,xt)],\Reg(T):=V^{\mathrm{UB}}-\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r^{0}(a_{t},x_{t})\right], (4)

where the expectation includes contexts, clean noise, learner randomness, and any randomized corruption.

Resource prices. To compare reward with resource use, assign nonnegative weights λ∈Λ:={λ∈ℝ+m:‖λ‖1≤1}\lambda\in\Lambda:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}:\|\lambda\|_{1}\leq 1\} and choose an overall scale Z>0Z>0. The weights have total mass at most one, and Z​λiZ\lambda_{i} is the price of one unit of resource ii in reward units. The clean Lagrangian score is expected reward minus priced expected consumption:

F0​(a,x,λ)=r0​(a,x)−Z​λ⊤​b0​(a,x).F^{0}(a,x;\lambda)=r^{0}(a,x)-Z\lambda^{\top}b^{0}(a,x).
{assumption}

[Lagrangian scale] Choose a positive scale Z>0Z>0 satisfying Z≥VUB/BminZ\geq V^{\mathrm{UB}}/B_{\min}, where Bmin=mini⁡BiB_{\min}=\min_{i}B_{i}.

The choice Z=T/BminZ=T/B_{\min} is computable from the horizon and budgets and satisfies Assumption 2.2 because VUB≤TV^{\mathrm{UB}}\leq T. This scale ensures that, in the stopping argument, depletion of any resource carries enough dual value to offset the remaining benchmark reward. Under proportional budgets, Bmin=Θ⁡(T)B_{\min}=\Theta(T) and Bmax:=maxi⁡Bi=O⁡(T)B_{\max}:=\max_{i}B_{i}=O(T), this choice gives Z=O⁡(1)Z=O(1). Our formal bounds nevertheless keep the dependence on these quantities explicit.

Effective corruption. Reward corruption changes the score directly; consumption corruption changes its resource-cost term. For every λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, the resulting score change satisfies

|ctr​(a)−Z​λ⊤​ctb​(a)|≤|ctr​(a)|+Z​‖ctb​(a)‖∞.\left|c_{t}^{r}(a)-Z\lambda^{\top}c_{t}^{b}(a)\right|\leq|c_{t}^{r}(a)|+Z\|c_{t}^{b}(a)\|_{\infty}. (5)

We therefore measure both types of corruption in the same units through the effective corruption budget

CZ:=∑t=1Tmaxa∈𝒜⁡{|ctr​(a)|+Z​‖ctb​(a)‖∞}.C_{Z}:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left\{|c_{t}^{r}(a)|+Z\|c_{t}^{b}(a)\|_{\infty}\right\}. (6)

The maximum covers all non-null actions before the fresh action draw on each round. In the known-corruption setting, the learner receives a deterministic bound Γ\Gamma satisfying CZ≤ΓC_{Z}\leq\Gamma on every admissible realization; in the unknown-corruption setting, no such bound is supplied. Knowing Γ\Gamma does not identify corrupted observations. For later analysis, we also measure corruption along the actions actually played:

Here CZ​(t)C_{Z}(t) measures both types of corruption in score units, whereas Cb​(t)C_{b}(t) measures only consumption corruption. Both use the selected actions, not the worst actions as in CZC_{Z}; in particular, CZ​(t)≤CZC_{Z}(t)\leq C_{Z}.

For estimation, let 𝒮aest​(t)\mathcal{S}_{a}^{\mathrm{est}}(t) contain the earlier rounds τ<t\tau<t when action aa was selected and its feedback retained for fitting (Section 3.1). The corresponding reward and resource-ii corruption totals are

Ca,estr​(t):=∑τ∈𝒮aest​(t)|cτr​(a)|,Ca,i,estb​(t):=∑τ∈𝒮aest​(t)|cτ,ib​(a)|.C_{a,\mathrm{est}}^{r}(t):=\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{S}_{a}^{\mathrm{est}}(t)}|c_{\tau}^{r}(a)|,\quad C_{a,i,\mathrm{est}}^{b}(t):=\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{S}_{a}^{\mathrm{est}}(t)}|c_{\tau,i}^{b}(a)|.

All these corruption quantities are for analysis: the learner cannot compute them without the clean outcomes.

2.3 Observed and Clean Budget Feasibility

Because the learner records observed consumption, its budget account may differ from clean resource use. Choose an operating budget 0<Bop≤B0<B^{\mathrm{op}}\leq B, with coordinatewise inequalities. This is the resource limit used by the algorithm; a smaller operating budget reserves a buffer against consumption corruption. Let Ut=∑τ<tbτ​(aτ)U_{t}=\sum_{\tau<t}b_{\tau}(a_{\tau}) be the observed use before round tt. A non-null action is allowed only if at least one unit remains in every operating budget, enough to cover any observed consumption on that round:

Ut,i≤Biop−1,∀i∈[m].U_{t,i}\leq B_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}-1,\quad\forall i\in[m]. (7)

Otherwise the learner selects 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null} from that round onward. The one-unit safety margin is already included in (7), so it is not subtracted again from BopB^{\mathrm{op}}. For [z]+:=max⁡{z,0}[z]_{+}:=\max\{z,0\}, define the largest observed and clean budget excesses relative to the original budget vector BB:

Violobs(T):=maxi∈[m][∑t=1Tbt,i(at)−Bi]+,Violcl(T):=maxi∈[m][∑t=1Tbt,icl(at)−Bi]+.\displaystyle\Viol_{\mathrm{obs}}(T):=\max_{i\in[m]}\Bigl[\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}(a_{t})-B_{i}\Bigr]_{+},\quad\Viol_{\mathrm{cl}}(T):=\max_{i\in[m]}\Bigl[\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a_{t})-B_{i}\Bigr]_{+}.

Recall that Cb​(T)C_{b}(T) is total consumption corruption along the played actions. Below, Γb\Gamma_{b} is an upper bound on this quantity, when available, and 𝟏{\bm{1}} is the all-ones vector. The guarantees hold on every realization.

Proposition 2.1 (Three feasibility levels)

Under (7), for every resource ii:

  1. (i)

    ∑t=1Tbt,i​(at)≤Biop\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}(a_{t})\leq B_{i}^{\mathrm{op}} (exact observed feasibility);

  2. (ii)

    ∑t=1Tbt,icl​(at)≤Biop+Cb​(T)\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a_{t})\leq B_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}+C_{b}(T) (clean sample-path control);

  3. (iii)

    if Cb​(T)≤ΓbC_{b}(T)\leq\Gamma_{b}, Bi>ΓbB_{i}>\Gamma_{b} for every ii, and Bop=B−Γb​𝟏B^{\mathrm{op}}=B-\Gamma_{b}{\bm{1}}, then ∑t=1Tbt,icl​(at)≤Bi\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a_{t})\leq B_{i} (strict clean sample-path feasibility).

Proof 2.2 (Proof)

Before a non-null action, the rule in (7) and bt,i​(at)≤1b_{t,i}(a_{t})\leq 1 imply that the updated observed use is at most BiopB_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}. Null actions use no resources, which proves (i). Since bt,icl​(at)=bt,i​(at)−ct,ib​(at)b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a_{t})=b_{t,i}(a_{t})-c_{t,i}^{b}(a_{t}),

∑t=1Tbt,icl​(at)≤∑t=1Tbt,i​(at)+∑t=1T|ct,ib​(at)|≤Biop+Cb​(T),\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a_{t})\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}(a_{t})+\sum_{t=1}^{T}|c_{t,i}^{b}(a_{t})|\leq B_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}+C_{b}(T),

which proves (ii). Substituting Biop=Bi−ΓbB_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}=B_{i}-\Gamma_{b} proves (iii).

For the default choice Bop=BB^{\mathrm{op}}=B, Proposition 2.1 gives

Violobs⁡(T)=0,Violcl⁡(T)≤Cb​(T)≤CZ/Z.\Viol_{\mathrm{obs}}(T)=0,\quad\Viol_{\mathrm{cl}}(T)\leq C_{b}(T)\leq C_{Z}/Z.

The last inequality follows because the per-round maximum defining CZC_{Z} dominates Z​‖ctb​(at)‖∞Z\|c_{t}^{b}(a_{t})\|_{\infty}. Hence CZ≤ΓC_{Z}\leq\Gamma also certifies Violcl⁡(T)≤Γ/Z\Viol_{\mathrm{cl}}(T)\leq\Gamma/Z. A corruption buffer protects clean feasibility but leaves fewer resources for reward. Let VUB​(B′)V^{\mathrm{UB}}(B^{\prime}) denote the population-LP value with budget vector B′B^{\prime}. To apply the regret guarantee with a reduced operating budget, first use that budget’s benchmark and a scale Z≥VUB​(Bop)/BminopZ\geq V^{\mathrm{UB}}(B^{\mathrm{op}})/B_{\min}^{\mathrm{op}}, where Bminop:=mini⁡BiopB_{\min}^{\mathrm{op}}:=\min_{i}B_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}; the computable choice Z=T/BminopZ=T/B_{\min}^{\mathrm{op}} is sufficient. All quantities that depend on ZZ, including the corruption allowance and confidence radii, use this same scale. Comparison with the original budget then adds VUB​(B)−VUB​(Bop)V^{\mathrm{UB}}(B)-V^{\mathrm{UB}}(B^{\mathrm{op}}); for the buffered choice, Bop=B−Γb​𝟏B^{\mathrm{op}}=B-\Gamma_{b}{\bm{1}}.

Remark 2.3 (Conditional-mean feasibility)

Proposition 2.1 controls clean realized consumptions bt,icl​(at)b_{t,i}^{\mathrm{cl}}(a_{t}), not their conditional means. To bound ∑tbi0​(at,xt)\sum_{t}b_{i}^{0}(a_{t},x_{t}), one must also account for clean stochastic noise. Under Assumption 2.1, a martingale concentration argument gives an additional buffer of order T​log⁡(m/δ)\sqrt{T\log(m/\delta)}, where δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) is the failure probability. Adding this concentration buffer gives the corresponding conditional-mean feasibility statement.

2.4 Notation Summary

3 Estimation and Optimistic Primal–Dual Learning

The method has two components: an estimator predicts reward and resource consumption, and an allocation rule uses these predictions and their uncertainty to choose actions and update resource prices. We first describe a norm-constrained Lasso estimator, then state the confidence and coverage requirements that connect estimation to regret, and finally give the allocation and price updates. The allocation guarantees depend on these requirements, not on Lasso itself. Calibration, proofs, and certified optimization details are in Appendix A.

3.1 Sparse Estimation and Prediction Confidence

For each non-null action, we fit one reward model and one model for each resource. A retained observation is an observation used in these fits. Forced exploration (FE) retains observations from context-independent uniform exploration; Shared-Grid also retains its fixed initialization samples. On-policy learning (OP) instead retains every non-null observation. All models for the same action use the same retained contexts.

Fix an action aa and one response, called a channel: reward with parameter θ⋆=μa⋆\theta^{\star}=\mu_{a}^{\star}, or consumption of resource ii with θ⋆=wa,i⋆\theta^{\star}=w_{a,i}^{\star}. Let 𝒮aest​(t)={τ<t:aτ=a​ and the sample is retained}\mathcal{S}_{a}^{\mathrm{est}}(t)=\{\tau<t:a_{\tau}=a\text{ and the sample is retained}\} be the retained round indices before tt, and let n=Naest​(t):=|𝒮aest​(t)|n=N_{a}^{\mathrm{est}}(t):=|\mathcal{S}_{a}^{\mathrm{est}}(t)|. The matrix X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} has the retained contexts as rows, and y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n} contains the corresponding observed responses.

For analysis, write y=X​θ⋆+η+ζy=X\theta^{\star}+\eta+\zeta, where η\eta is clean stochastic noise and ζ\zeta collects the post-clipping corruptions. The learner observes XX and yy, not the separate noise and corruption terms. Whether to retain a sample is decided before its feedback is revealed.

For regularization strength ρn>0\rho_{n}>0, we use the norm-constrained Lasso fit (tibshirani1996lasso):

θ^∈arg​min‖θ‖2≤R⁡{‖y−X​θ‖222​n+ρn​‖θ‖1},n≥1.\widehat{\theta}\in\argmin_{\|\theta\|_{2}\leq R}\left\{\frac{\|y-X\theta\|_{2}^{2}}{2n}+\rho_{n}\|\theta\|_{1}\right\},\quad n\geq 1. (8)

The ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty encourages sparse estimates, while the ℓ2\ell_{2} constraint enforces the known coefficient bound RR. Neither fixes the support of the estimate. Set θ^=0\widehat{\theta}=0 when n=0n=0.

The prediction guarantee uses a supplied sparsity bound s≥max⁡{1,s0}s\geq\max\{1,s_{0}\}, a retained-sample threshold n0n_{0}, and an estimation failure level δest∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{est}}\in(0,1). The bound ss calibrates confidence and numerical precision; it is not a support constraint in the fit. The retained design is the matrix of contexts used by that fit. Its restricted strong convexity (RSC) condition requires those contexts to distinguish changes in the coefficient vector, with an ℓ1\ell_{1} tolerance for high-dimensional data. The constant κ>0\kappa>0 measures the curvature in this condition; the precise inequality is (47).

Appendix A.2 specifies ρn,κ,n0\rho_{n},\kappa,n_{0}, and Appendix A.8 specifies how accurately to solve the objective. For a fixed retained history, the fitted coefficients and regularization do not depend on a proposed corruption bound Γ\Gamma. Such a bound changes the confidence radii, not the fitting objective.

Proposition 3.1 (Prediction confidence for the concrete estimator)

Under Assumption 2.1 and the calibration specified in Appendix A.2, there is a noise event of probability at least 1−δest1-\delta_{\mathrm{est}}, simultaneous over actions, response channels, and obtained sample prefixes. On this event, whenever a retained prefix n≥n0n\geq n_{0} satisfies the calibrated RSC condition, any feasible fit meeting the certified optimization tolerance of Appendix A.8 satisfies

sup‖x‖2≤1|⟨θ^−θ⋆,x⟩|≤min⁡{2​R,7​ρn​sκ+4​Cnκ​n},Cn:=‖ζ‖1.\sup_{\|x\|_{2}\leq 1}|\langle\widehat{\theta}-\theta^{\star},x\rangle|\leq\min\left\{2R,\,\frac{7\rho_{n}\sqrt{s}}{\kappa}+\frac{4C_{n}}{\kappa n}\right\},\quad C_{n}:=\|\zeta\|_{1}. (9)

For an exact minimizer, the coefficient 77 can be replaced by 66.

Here CnC_{n} measures corruption only in the retained responses for this action and channel. The term 7​ρn​s/κ7\rho_{n}\sqrt{s}/\kappa is the clean estimation contribution: ρn\rho_{n} decreases as n−1/2n^{-1/2} under the stated calibration, s\sqrt{s} reflects sparsity, and 1/κ1/\kappa reflects design conditioning. The additional term 4​Cn/(κ​n)4C_{n}/(\kappa n) measures the effect of retained corruption. The cap 2​R2R follows from the norm constraint, and the coefficient 77, rather than 66, allows the certified numerical error. Appendix A.5 gives the proof, including the large-corruption case.

3.2 Coverage and the Estimator Interface

The allocation rule needs predictions and confidence radii from estimator. Write μ^a,t−1\widehat{\mu}_{a,t-1} and w^a,i,t−1\widehat{w}_{a,i,t-1} for the reward and resource fits using observations before round tt. At the current context, their clipped predictions are r^a,t=clip⁡(⟨μ^a,t−1,xt⟩,0,1)\widehat{r}_{a,t}=\clip(\langle\widehat{\mu}_{a,t-1},x_{t}\rangle,0,1) and b^a,i,t=clip⁡(⟨w^a,i,t−1,xt⟩,0,1)\widehat{b}_{a,i,t}=\clip(\langle\widehat{w}_{a,i,t-1},x_{t}\rangle,0,1). The interface imposes two requirements: the radii must cover prediction errors, and the uncertainty charged over the run must be controlled.

Pointwise prediction confidence. A corruption candidate Γ\Gamma is a proposed upper bound on CZC_{Z}; it is valid when Γ≥CZ\Gamma\geq C_{Z}. Let βa,tr,Γ\beta_{a,t}^{r,\Gamma} and βa,i,tb,Γ\beta_{a,i,t}^{b,\Gamma} be nonnegative error radii for the reward and resource-ii predictions. These radii bound errors in clean conditional means, not errors relative to the noisy observed feedback. Predictions and radii use the observed history and xtx_{t} and are fixed before the fresh action draw. On a common retained history, candidates share point estimates and differ only in their radii.

Let δcov∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}\in(0,1) be the failure level for the design/coverage event. On one joint event of failure at most δest+δcov\delta_{\mathrm{est}}+\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}, require simultaneously for every valid Γ≥CZ\Gamma\geq C_{Z},

|r^a,t−r0(a,xt)|≤βa,tr,Γ,|b^a,i,t−bi0(a,xt)|≤βa,i,tb,Γ(a∈𝒜,i∈[m],t∈[T]).|\widehat{r}_{a,t}-r^{0}(a,x_{t})|\leq\beta_{a,t}^{r,\Gamma},\quad|\widehat{b}_{a,i,t}-b_{i}^{0}(a,x_{t})|\leq\beta_{a,i,t}^{b,\Gamma}\quad(a\in\mathcal{A},\ i\in[m],\ t\in[T]). (10)

For Lasso, Proposition 3.1 and CZ≤ΓC_{Z}\leq\Gamma give the radii in Appendix A.4; use unit radii before n0n_{0} and zero predictions and radii for 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null}. The allocation rule compares reward minus resource cost. Its combined radius therefore adds reward uncertainty to resource uncertainty in the same units. Since ‖λ‖1≤1\|\lambda\|_{1}\leq 1, the largest resource radius suffices. Write hh for the length of the clean-score interval [−Z,1][-Z,1]:

βa,tZ,Γ:=βa,tr,Γ+Z​maxi​βa,i,tb,Γ,h:=1+Z.\beta_{a,t}^{Z,\Gamma}:=\beta_{a,t}^{r,\Gamma}+Z\max_{i}\beta_{a,i,t}^{b,\Gamma},\quad h:=1+Z. (11)

Cumulative uncertainty. Pointwise confidence alone is not enough for a regret bound: the widths charged over the run must also remain small. Let a^t\widehat{a}_{t} denote the optimistic recommendation defined in Section 3.3, with the fixed corruption input suppressed in this notation. Let It∈{0,1}I_{t}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether the pre-action safety test (7) passes; it remains one on an active round even if 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null} is subsequently chosen. Require on the same event

2​∑t=1TIt​βa^t,tZ,Γ≤ℛest0+ψest​(Γ).2\sum_{t=1}^{T}I_{t}\beta_{\widehat{a}_{t},t}^{Z,\Gamma}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{est}}^{0}+\psi_{\mathrm{est}}(\Gamma). (12)

Here ℛest0\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{est}}^{0} bounds cumulative uncertainty from clean estimation, and ψest​(Γ)\psi_{\mathrm{est}}(\Gamma) bounds the additional width caused by retained corruption. Both are analysis quantities, not algorithm inputs. The optimistic comparison charges uncertainty to the recommended action, so no separate cumulative-width bound is needed along the population-LP policy. Shared-Grid needs the corresponding bound uniformly over valid candidates on one shared history; see (30). Any estimator meeting these confidence and cumulative-width requirements can replace Lasso without changing the allocation analysis.

Design conditions for the concrete rates. The conditions below establish the interface for Lasso; the general allocation theorem does not impose them on another estimator that already meets the interface. FE selects its retained actions independently of the current context on active rounds, allowing a population condition to control the retained designs. OP uses adaptively selected observations and instead requires a condition on its actual retained designs. Restricted-curvature conditions are standard in sparse estimation (negahban2012unified, raskutti2010restricted), but adaptive action selection must also be accounted for (bastani2020online). Appendix A.3 gives the calibrations and proofs.

{assumption}

[Population design for the concrete estimator] For a generic context x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}, known constants κx,Lx>0\kappa_{x},L_{x}>0 satisfy

𝔼[xx⊤]⪰κxId,𝔼exp(⟨u,x⟩2Lx2​‖u‖22)≤2(u≠0).\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}]\succeq\kappa_{x}I_{d},\quad\mathbb{E}\exp\left(\frac{\langle u,x\rangle^{2}}{L_{x}^{2}\|u\|_{2}^{2}}\right)\leq 2\quad(u\neq 0). (13)

Here κx\kappa_{x} lower-bounds the eigenvalues of the population second-moment matrix 𝔼⁡[x​x⊤]\mathbb{E}[xx^{\top}], while LxL_{x} controls the directional sub-Gaussian scale.

For OP, the relevant information is in the contexts actually retained for each action, rather than in the population distribution alone.

Condition \theassumption (On-policy retained-design coverage)

For supplied design parameters κop,υop>0\kappa_{\mathrm{op}},\upsilon_{\mathrm{op}}>0 and threshold n0n_{0}, the action-specific realized retained designs satisfy the calibrated RSC event defined in Appendix A.3, simultaneously after n0n_{0} samples per action, with probability at least 1−δcov1-\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}. Here κop\kappa_{\mathrm{op}} is the RSC curvature and υop\upsilon_{\mathrm{op}} controls its ℓ1\ell_{1} tolerance.

This condition concerns the algorithm’s actual adaptive, corrupted, and potentially stopped trajectory; population richness alone does not imply it. Shared-Grid OP also needs the separate recommendation-coverage condition in Section 5, because a candidate may recommend an action that is not played.

Rate constants. The concrete regret bounds use ℓ:=log⁡(16​e​K​(m+1)​d​T/min⁡{δest,δcov})\ell:=\log\bigl(16eK(m+1)dT/\min\{\delta_{\mathrm{est}},\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}\}\bigr) for concentration and HT:=1+log⁡(1+T)H_{T}:=1+\log(1+T) for the harmonic factor arising when widths are summed. The retained-design curvatures are κFE:=κx/2\kappa_{\mathrm{FE}}:=\kappa_{x}/2 for FE and κop\kappa_{\mathrm{op}} from Condition 3.2 for OP. The coefficients AFEA_{\mathrm{FE}} and AopA_{\mathrm{op}} multiply the corresponding corruption-free n−1/2n^{-1/2} score widths. They include model and design parameters, not just universal constants; Appendix A.3 gives their full dependence.

3.3 Optimistic Primal–Dual Rule

The primal step recommends an action using estimated reward minus resource cost, with an uncertainty bonus. The dual step adjusts resource prices using the consumption actually observed.

At prices λt∈Λ\lambda_{t}\in\Lambda, substitute the fitted reward and consumption means into the clean score F0​(a,xt,λt)F^{0}(a,x_{t};\lambda_{t}). This gives the estimated score F^a,t\widehat{F}_{a,t}; candidate Γ\Gamma recommends the action with the largest estimate plus its confidence radius:

F^a,t​(λt)\displaystyle\widehat{F}_{a,t}(\lambda_{t}) :=r^a,t−Z​∑i=1mλt,i​b^a,i,t,\displaystyle:=\widehat{r}_{a,t}-Z\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_{t,i}\widehat{b}_{a,i,t}, (14)
a^tΓ\displaystyle\widehat{a}_{t}^{\Gamma} ∈arg​maxa∈𝒜0⁡{F^a,t​(λt)+βa,tZ,Γ},\displaystyle\in\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{0}}\{\widehat{F}_{a,t}(\lambda_{t})+\beta_{a,t}^{Z,\Gamma}\}, (15)

with zero score and radius for 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null} and the fixed order 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕,1,…,K\mathtt{null},1,\ldots,K for ties. a^tΓ\widehat{a}_{t}^{\Gamma} is the optimistic recommendation for candidate Γ\Gamma, computed on rounds that pass the pre-action safety test (7). The actually played action ata_{t} may differ because of forced exploration or the Shared-Grid master; if the safety test fails, the learner plays 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null} from that round onward.

For the price update, represent λt\lambda_{t} by the first mm coordinates of a probability vector qt∈ℝ+m+1q_{t}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m+1}: λt=qt,1:m\lambda_{t}=q_{t,1:m} and qt,m+1=1−‖λt‖1q_{t,m+1}=1-\|\lambda_{t}\|_{1}. The last coordinate holds unused price mass; it is not another physical resource. Compare observed consumption with the per-round operating-budget target Bop/TB^{\mathrm{op}}/T. For stepsize ηq>0\eta_{q}>0, set g~t=(bt​(at)−Bop/T,0)\widetilde{g}_{t}=(b_{t}(a_{t})-B^{\mathrm{op}}/T,0), with zero in the slack coordinate, and update

qt+1,j∝qt,jeηq​g~t,j,λt+1=qt+1,1:m.q_{t+1,j}\propto q_{t,j}e^{\eta_{q}\widetilde{g}_{t,j}},\quad\lambda_{t+1}=q_{t+1,1:m}. (16)

Normalize qt+1q_{t+1} to sum to one. The update increases the relative weight of resources with larger excess use. We denote its cumulative price-learning penalty by

𝒟T:=Z⁡[log⁡(m+1)ηq+ηq​(1+BmaxT)2​T].\mathcal{D}_{T}:=Z\left[\frac{\log(m+1)}{\eta_{q}}+\eta_{q}\left(1+\frac{B_{\max}}{T}\right)^{2}T\right]. (17)

Choosing ηq≍log⁡(m+1)/T1+Bmax/T\eta_{q}\asymp\frac{\sqrt{\log(m+1)/T}}{1+B_{\max}/T} gives 𝒟T=O⁡(Z⁡(1+BmaxT)​T​log⁡(m+1))\mathcal{D}_{T}=O\left(Z\left(1+\frac{B_{\max}}{T}\right)\sqrt{T\log(m+1)}\right).

4 Robust Learning with Known Corruption

4.1 Algorithm and Inputs

We now assume that the learner receives a deterministic bound Γ≥CZ\Gamma\geq C_{Z} that is valid on every admissible realization. On each active round, ROPD forms an optimistic recommendation, selects an action, and updates its estimates, resource prices, and observed-budget account from the played action’s feedback. Forced exploration may replace the recommendation by a uniform non-null action; on-policy learning plays the recommendation.

Using the fitted score and radius from Section 3, write the optimistic score as

Ua,tΓ:=F^a,t​(λt)+βa,tZ,Γ,U_{a,t}^{\Gamma}:=\widehat{F}_{a,t}(\lambda_{t})+\beta_{a,t}^{Z,\Gamma}, (18)

with U𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕,tΓ=0U_{\mathtt{null},t}^{\Gamma}=0. Here Ua,tΓU_{a,t}^{\Gamma} is a scalar optimistic score for action aa, distinct from the cumulative observed-consumption vector UtU_{t}.

In FE mode, ϵt\epsilon_{t} is the probability of a uniform forced action at round tt, and only forced observations are retained for estimation. OP retains every non-null observation and sets ϵt=0\epsilon_{t}=0. For a fixed retained history, Γ\Gamma changes confidence radii but not the fitting objective; it can still affect future data through action selection.

Table 4 lists the inputs, and Algorithm 1 gives the complete procedure. In the algorithm, ℋa,test\mathcal{H}_{a,t}^{\mathrm{est}} denotes action aa’s retained data through round tt, so |ℋa,t−1est|=Naest​(t)|\mathcal{H}_{a,t-1}^{\mathrm{est}}|=N_{a}^{\mathrm{est}}(t). The concrete fits are specified in Section 3.1 and Appendix A.2. Another estimator meeting the interface can replace these fits without changing the allocation, price, or safety updates.

The pre-action check leaves room for one more observed consumption, since bt,i​(at)≤1b_{t,i}(a_{t})\leq 1. It therefore gives exact observed feasibility, ∑t=1Tbt,i​(at)≤Biop\sum_{t=1}^{T}b_{t,i}(a_{t})\leq B_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}. If a valid bound Cb​(T)≤ΓbC_{b}(T)\leq\Gamma_{b} is known and Bi>ΓbB_{i}>\Gamma_{b} for every resource, using Bop=B−Γb​𝟏B^{\mathrm{op}}=B-\Gamma_{b}{\bm{1}} also gives strict clean sample-path feasibility by Proposition 2.1.

The regret guarantees below use the default budget Bop=BB^{\mathrm{op}}=B. For a reduced operating budget, first apply the analysis to the reduced-budget benchmark, with Z≥VUB​(Bop)/BminopZ\geq V^{\mathrm{UB}}(B^{\mathrm{op}})/B_{\min}^{\mathrm{op}}, where Bminop:=mini⁡BiopB_{\min}^{\mathrm{op}}:=\min_{i}B_{i}^{\mathrm{op}}; Z=T/BminopZ=T/B_{\min}^{\mathrm{op}} is sufficient. Evaluate all scale-dependent quantities, including CZC_{Z} and its supplied bound Γ\Gamma, with this same scale. Returning to the original benchmark then adds VUB​(B)−VUB​(Bop)V^{\mathrm{UB}}(B)-V^{\mathrm{UB}}(B^{\mathrm{op}}), as explained in Appendix B. This scale qualification is needed for the regret analysis, not for the pathwise feasibility statement. For the default-budget price update, the stepsize choice from Section 3.3 gives

𝒟T=O⁡(Z⁡(1+BmaxT)​T​log⁡(m+1)).\mathcal{D}_{T}=O\left(Z(1+\frac{B_{\max}}{T})\sqrt{T\log(m+1)}\right). (19)

4.2 Regret and Resource Guarantees

The first guarantee separates estimation uncertainty from exploration, price learning, direct corruption, and stopping. Set δtot:=δest+δcov\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\delta_{\mathrm{est}}+\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}, combining estimator and coverage failure probabilities.

Theorem 4.1 (Known corruption: regret and resource control)

Suppose Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 hold and the estimator/coverage pair satisfies the interface in (10)–(12) for a deterministic supplied bound Γ\Gamma with CZ≤ΓC_{Z}\leq\Gamma on every admissible realization. Algorithm 1 with Bop=BB^{\mathrm{op}}=B satisfies the following expected-regret bound:

Reg⁡(T)≤O⁡(ℛest0+h​∑t=1Tϵt+𝒟T+Γ+ψest​(Γ)+Z)+h​δtot​T.\Reg(T)\leq O\left(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{est}}^{0}+h\sum_{t=1}^{T}\epsilon_{t}+\mathcal{D}_{T}+\Gamma+\psi_{\mathrm{est}}(\Gamma)+Z\right)+h\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}T. (20)

Moreover, on every realization, Violobs⁡(T)=0\Viol_{\mathrm{obs}}(T)=0 and Violcl⁡(T)≤Cb​(T)≤CZ/Z≤Γ/Z\Viol_{\mathrm{cl}}(T)\leq C_{b}(T)\leq C_{Z}/Z\leq\Gamma/Z.

Proof overview. In (20), ℛest0\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{est}}^{0} measures clean estimation uncertainty, h​∑tϵth\sum_{t}\epsilon_{t} the cost of forced exploration, and 𝒟T\mathcal{D}_{T} the cost of learning resource prices. Corruption enters in two distinct ways: Γ\Gamma accounts for transferring corrupted scores and resource use to their clean counterparts, while ψest​(Γ)\psi_{\mathrm{est}}(\Gamma) accounts for its accumulated effect on prediction widths. The term ZZ is the stopping boundary, and h​δtot​Th\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}T is the failure-event cost. Confidence controls the clean-score gap, the price update controls observed resource imbalance, and Z​Bi≥VUBZB_{i}\geq V^{\mathrm{UB}} offsets benchmark reward lost after stopping. Appendix B gives the full argument.

4.3 Concrete Rates

The next corollary instantiates the theorem with Lasso. FE collects context-independent exploration samples and pays an exploration cost. OP uses all non-null observations but requires the realized-design condition; its sharper rate is not asserted under the FE assumptions alone.

Corollary 4.2 (Known corruption: concrete rates)

Under Assumptions 2.1–2.2, run Algorithm 1 with Bop=BB^{\mathrm{op}}=B, a deterministic valid bound Γ≥CZ\Gamma\geq C_{Z}, and the estimator and certified precision of Proposition 3.1. For a universal CC, with the rate constants defined in Section 3.2:

  1. (i)

    Forced exploration. Under the population-design Assumption 3.2 (calibration in Appendix A.3), use (49) and a constant forced-exploration probability ϵt≡ϵ\epsilon_{t}\equiv\epsilon chosen by (50). Then

    Reg(T)≤C[\displaystyle\Reg(T)\leq C\biggl[ h1/3​AFE2/3​K1/3​T2/3+h​K⁡(n0+ℓ)​T\displaystyle h^{1/3}A_{\mathrm{FE}}^{2/3}K^{1/3}T^{2/3}+h\sqrt{K(n_{0}+\ell)T} (21)
    +(1+K​HTκFE​ϵ)Γ+𝒟T+Z]+hδtotT.\displaystyle+\left(1+\frac{KH_{T}}{\kappa_{\mathrm{FE}}\epsilon}\right)\Gamma+\mathcal{D}_{T}+Z\biggr]+h\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}T.
  2. (ii)

    On-policy learning. Under the retained-design Condition 3.2, with ϵt=0\epsilon_{t}=0, use the supplied OP calibration and the same certified Lasso rule on all non-null samples. Then

    Reg(T)≤C[\displaystyle\Reg(T)\leq C\biggl[ AopK​T+hKn0+(1+K​HTκop)Γ+𝒟T+Z]+hδtotT.\displaystyle A_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt{KT}+hKn_{0}+\left(1+\frac{KH_{T}}{\kappa_{\mathrm{op}}}\right)\Gamma+\mathcal{D}_{T}+Z\biggr]+h\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}T. (22)

The terms involving AFEA_{\mathrm{FE}} or AopA_{\mathrm{op}} measure clean learning, and the n0n_{0} terms account for the initial period before informative confidence is available. The terms proportional to Γ\Gamma measure corruption’s additional effect under the corresponding design conditioning. Price learning, stopping, and failure events contribute the same 𝒟T+Z+h​δtot​T\mathcal{D}_{T}+Z+h\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}T terms as in the theorem.

With proportional budgets, fixed remaining parameters, dominated burn-in, the stepsize following (17), and δtot≤T−2\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}\leq T^{-2}, the FE and OP bounds simplify to O~​(T2/3+Γ​T1/3)\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3}+\Gamma T^{1/3}) and O~​(T+Γ)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}+\Gamma), respectively. Here O~\widetilde{O} suppresses polylogarithmic factors in d,K,m,Td,K,m,T and inverse failure levels. Appendix B.6 gives full analysis.

Comparison of rates. Reward-corrupted linear bandits without resource constraints achieve near-optimal or minimax corruption dependence (he2022nearly, liu2024corruption), while clean sparse CBwK exhibits T2/3T^{2/3}-type learning costs and, under stronger coverage, T\sqrt{T} behavior (ma2023high). Our results extend these CBwK regimes to joint reward and consumption corruption, giving O~​(T2/3+Γ​T1/3)\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3}+\Gamma T^{1/3}) under FE and O~​(T+Γ)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}+\Gamma) under OP, together with observed-budget feasibility and control of clean resource violation. The rates are not directly comparable across settings and no matching lower bound establishes their optimality.

4.4 Exploration Tradeoff and the Clean Case

The preceding FE rate uses a calibrated exploration probability. The next result keeps ϵ\epsilon explicit, showing the tradeoff between collecting informative samples and the reward cost of exploration.

Corollary 4.3 (Known FE with a calibrated estimator)

Under Assumptions 2.1, 2.2, and 3.2, run Algorithm 1 with Bop=BB^{\mathrm{op}}=B, a deterministic pathwise bound CZ≤ΓC_{Z}\leq\Gamma, constant 0<ϵ≤1/20<\epsilon\leq 1/2, and (49). Use the regularization, trivial early radii, and certified numerical precision of Appendix A.2. For a universal CC and δtot=δest+δcov\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}=\delta_{\mathrm{est}}+\delta_{\mathrm{cov}},

Reg(T)≤C[\displaystyle\Reg(T)\leq C\biggl[ h​K​(n0+ℓ)ϵ+AFE​K​Tϵ+h​ϵ​T\displaystyle\frac{hK(n_{0}+\ell)}{\epsilon}+A_{\mathrm{FE}}\sqrt{\frac{KT}{\epsilon}}+h\epsilon T (23)
+𝒟T+Γ+K​Γ​HTκFE​ϵ+Z]+hδtotT.\displaystyle+\mathcal{D}_{T}+\Gamma+\frac{K\Gamma H_{T}}{\kappa_{\mathrm{FE}}\epsilon}+Z\biggr]+h\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}T.

The bound holds for every T≥1T\geq 1, even if coverage is not reached. The choice (50) gives the main-text bound (21), by the calculation in Appendix B.6.

In (23), smaller ϵ\epsilon reduces the exploration cost h​ϵ​Th\epsilon T but increases the initial coverage and estimation costs, including the corruption-dependent width. The choice (50) balances the clean terms and does not depend on Γ\Gamma; the corruption term is evaluated at that choice. The bound remains valid at short horizons, but need not be informative before enough samples are collected.

OP has no forced-exploration parameter. Setting both the actual corruption and the supplied allowance to zero gives the following special case of its bound.

Corollary 4.4 (Clean known-corruption case)

Under the on-policy conditions of Corollary 4.2 with CZ=Γ=0C_{Z}=\Gamma=0, the Γ\Gamma-dependent contribution in (22) vanishes. The burn-in, numerical/statistical width, dual term, stopping boundary, and h​δtot​Th\delta_{\mathrm{tot}}T remain.

These claims follow by substituting Lemma A.14 or Proposition A.18 into the modular known-corruption theorem; Appendix B proves the allocation step. In particular, no sparsity-constrained optimizer or empirical sparse-eigenvalue oracle is used.

5 Adaptation to Unknown Corruption

Without a supplied corruption bound, Shared-Grid considers several possible bounds, called candidates, and uses a master to combine their recommendations into one action distribution. Candidates share the retained data, fitted coefficients, resource prices, and budget account; only their confidence radii and recommendations differ. They are not separate runs of ROPD: each round produces one played action and at most one retained observation.

5.1 Candidates and Shared Estimation

Corruption candidates. A candidate Γ\Gamma uses the optimistic recommendation (15) with the common fits and its own radius βa,tZ,Γ\beta_{a,t}^{Z,\Gamma}. The post-clipping bounds imply CZ≤Cmax,Z:=T⁡(1+Z)C_{Z}\leq C_{\max,Z}:=T(1+Z), so zero and successive powers of two cover all admissible corruption levels:

𝒢:={0}∪{2j:j=0,…,⌈log2Cmax,Z⌉}.\mathcal{G}:=\{0\}\cup\{2^{j}:j=0,\ldots,\lceil\log_{2}C_{\max,Z}\rceil\}. (24)

The learner uses every candidate without knowing which are valid. For analysis, define

Γ⋆:=min⁡{Γ∈𝒢:Γ≥CZ}.\Gamma^{\star}:=\min\{\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}:\Gamma\geq C_{Z}\}. (25)

It satisfies

Γ⋆=0​if ​CZ=0,CZ≤Γ⋆≤max⁡{1,2​CZ}​otherwise.\Gamma^{\star}=0\ \text{if }C_{Z}=0,\qquad C_{Z}\leq\Gamma^{\star}\leq\max\{1,2C_{Z}\}\ \text{otherwise}. (26)

The comparator Γ⋆\Gamma^{\star} is determined by the realized path, not supplied to or computed by the learner. Its recommendations use the common realized history, not a counterfactual history from running that candidate alone.

Initialization and retained samples. Begin with a prescribed cyclic schedule over the KK non-null actions, of length tinit≤Tt_{\mathrm{init}}\leq T, a nonnegative multiple of KK. The schedule is fixed before the current context and feedback, and every round must pass the safety test (7); failure stops non-null play and freezes all states. Initialization observations are retained and update prices and the budget account, but not master weights.

After initialization, forced-exploration (FE) mode overrides the master with probability ϵt\epsilon_{t} and selects uniformly from the non-null actions. Let et=1e_{t}=1 mark this override; in on-policy (OP) mode, ϵt=et=0\epsilon_{t}=e_{t}=0. Recall that It=1I_{t}=1 means the safety test passes, even if 𝚗𝚞𝚕𝚕\mathtt{null} is then chosen. The shared retained set for action aa before round tt is

ℐa,test={{τ<t:Iτ=1,aτ=a,[τ≤tinitoreτ=1]},𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾=𝖿𝗈𝗋𝖼𝖾𝖽,{τ<t:Iτ=1,aτ=a},𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾=𝗈𝗇​-​𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗒.\mathcal{I}_{a,t}^{\mathrm{est}}=\begin{cases}\{\tau<t:I_{\tau}=1,\ a_{\tau}=a,\ [\tau\leq t_{\mathrm{init}}\ \text{or}\ e_{\tau}=1]\},&\mathsf{mode}=\mathsf{forced},\\ \{\tau<t:I_{\tau}=1,\ a_{\tau}=a\},&\mathsf{mode}=\mathsf{on\mbox{-}policy}.\end{cases} (27)

Thus FE retains initialization and forced samples, whereas OP retains every non-null observation. Eligibility is decided before feedback. Each eligible observation is appended once, and all candidates use the same regularization, numerical precision, supplied calibration, and fits.

5.2 Master and Complete Procedure

Advice and sampling. The EXP4.P master (beygelzimer2011contextual) combines experts, each supplying an action distribution called its advice. Set K0:=|𝒜0|=K+1K_{0}:=|\mathcal{A}_{0}|=K+1 and ℰM:=𝒢∪{unif}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{M}}:=\mathcal{G}\cup\{\mathrm{unif}\}, with M:=|𝒢|+1M:=|\mathcal{G}|+1. Candidate Γ\Gamma gives advice ξt,Γ(a)=𝟏{a^tΓ=a}\xi_{t,\Gamma}(a)=\bm{1}\{\widehat{a}_{t}^{\Gamma}=a\}; the extra expert gives ξt,unif​(a)=1/K0\xi_{t,\mathrm{unif}}(a)=1/K_{0}, as required by beygelzimer2011contextual. Advice ξt,j\xi_{t,j} is distinct from corruption; the extra expert requires no fit.

Expert weights wt,jw_{t,j} start at one. Their normalized values wt,j/Wtw_{t,j}/W_{t}, where Wt:=∑jwt,jW_{t}:=\sum_{j}w_{t,j}, weight the advice in the master’s action distribution ptp_{t}. For failure level δmaster\delta_{\mathrm{master}}, use probability floor pminp_{\min} and confidence-bonus coefficient αm\alpha_{m}:

pmin:=min⁡{12​K0,log⁡MK0​T},αm:=log⁡(3​M/δmaster)K0​T.p_{\min}:=\min\left\{\frac{1}{2K_{0}},\sqrt{\frac{\log M}{K_{0}T}}\right\},\quad\alpha_{m}:=\sqrt{\frac{\log(3M/\delta_{\mathrm{master}})}{K_{0}T}}. (28)

The uniform expert supplies advice, smoothing ensures pt​(a)≥pminp_{t}(a)\geq p_{\min}, and forced exploration supplies independent FE samples. The distribution ptp_{t} applies only on the non-forced branch.

Payoffs and updates. The master evaluates reward net of current resource cost and rescales this score to [0,1][0,1]:

Ftobs​(a,λt):=rt​(a)−Z​λt⊤​bt​(a),Yt​(a):=Ftobs​(a,λt)+Z1+Z,a∈𝒜0.F_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}}(a;\lambda_{t}):=r_{t}(a)-Z\lambda_{t}^{\top}b_{t}(a),\quad Y_{t}(a):=\frac{F_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}}(a;\lambda_{t})+Z}{1+Z},\quad a\in\mathcal{A}_{0}. (29)

Since Ftobs∈[−Z,1]F_{t}^{\mathrm{obs}}\in[-Z,1], Yt∈[0,1]Y_{t}\in[0,1]. Only the played action’s feedback is observed. On a non-forced active round after initialization, importance weighting divides its payoff by pt​(at)p_{t}(a_{t}) to correct for unequal sampling probabilities. Algorithm 2 defines the action-payoff estimate Y^t​(a)\widehat{Y}_{t}(a), its advice-weighted expert estimate y^t,j\widehat{y}_{t,j}, and the inverse-probability bonus term v^t,j\widehat{v}_{t,j}.

The complete procedure below uses the shared estimator, including trivial early radii. Expert weights wt,jw_{t,j} combine advice; price weights qtq_{t} govern resources. Initialization and overrides freeze expert weights, but prices and accounting update from observed consumption on every active round.

5.3 Confidence and Recommendation Coverage

A common confidence event. Because Γ⋆\Gamma^{\star} depends on the realized path, the analysis needs one event covering every valid candidate. Shared fits, the time-uniform noise event, and calibrated retained designs give simultaneous pointwise confidence; the cumulative requirement is

2​∑t=tinit+1TIt​βa^tΓ,tZ,Γ≤ℛsh0+ψest​(Γ).2\sum_{t=t_{\mathrm{init}}+1}^{T}I_{t}\beta_{\widehat{a}_{t}^{\Gamma},t}^{Z,\Gamma}\leq\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sh}}^{0}+\psi_{\mathrm{est}}(\Gamma). (30)

This inequality must hold for all valid Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G} on the same event. Here ℛsh0\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sh}}^{0} bounds corruption-free recommendation widths after initialization, and ψest​(Γ)\psi_{\mathrm{est}}(\Gamma) is their additional corruption cost. The common event and radii monotone in Γ\Gamma permit substitution of Γ⋆\Gamma^{\star} after the run; Appendix C gives the argument.

Why OP needs recommendation coverage. A candidate may repeatedly recommend an action that the master rarely plays. Retained-design coverage controls the quality of that action’s data, but does not ensure enough observations for its recommendations. Let Na(t):=∑τ<t𝟏{aτ=a}N_{a}(t):=\sum_{\tau<t}\bm{1}\{a_{\tau}=a\} count actual plays, including initialization, and let Narec,Γ(t):=∑τ=tinit+1t−1Iτ𝟏{a^τΓ=a}N_{a}^{\mathrm{rec},\Gamma}(t):=\sum_{\tau=t_{\mathrm{init}}+1}^{t-1}I_{\tau}\bm{1}\{\widehat{a}_{\tau}^{\Gamma}=a\} count post-initialization active recommendations. The following condition relates the two counts.

Condition \theassumption (Covered recommendations)

For a recommendation-to-play ratio χ≥1\chi\geq 1, additive count slack ncand≥0n_{\mathrm{cand}}\geq 0, and failure level δcand∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{cand}}\in(0,1),

ℙ⁡(Narec,Γ​(t)≤ncand+χ​Na​(t)​for all Γ∈𝒢, a∈𝒜, and t≤T+1)≥1−δcand.{\mathbb{P}}\left(N_{a}^{\mathrm{rec},\Gamma}(t)\leq n_{\mathrm{cand}}+\chi N_{a}(t)\ \text{for all $\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}$, $a\in\mathcal{A}$, and $t\leq T+1$}\right)\geq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{cand}}. (31)

The ratio χ\chi and slack ncandn_{\mathrm{cand}} ensure that frequent recommendations are supported by actual plays. This complements the OP retained-design Condition 3.2; FE instead obtains candidate-independent samples through uniform exploration and does not need this extra condition. Both OP conditions concern the actual shared trajectory, not a post-run diagnostic. The next lemma gives sufficient sampling probabilities.

Suppose that on every post-initialization active round in on-policy mode, a candidate-recommended action receives conditional sampling probability at least qcov>0q_{\mathrm{cov}}>0: whenever a^tΓ=a\widehat{a}_{t}^{\Gamma}=a,

ℙ⁡(at=a∣𝒬t)≥qcov,{\mathbb{P}}(a_{t}=a\mid\mathcal{Q}_{t})\geq q_{\mathrm{cov}},

where 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t} contains the history, current context, shared estimates, prices, and all candidate recommendations before the fresh action draw. Then, with probability at least 1−δcand1-\delta_{\mathrm{cand}}, simultaneously for every Γ∈𝒢\Gamma\in\mathcal{G}, a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and t≤T+1t\leq T+1,

Narec,Γ​(t)≤2qcov​Na​(t)+8qcov​log⁡2​|𝒢|​K​Tδcand.N_{a}^{\mathrm{rec},\Gamma}(t)\leq\frac{2}{q_{\mathrm{cov}}}N_{a}(t)+\frac{8}{q_{\mathrm{cov}}}\log\frac{2|\mathcal{G}|KT}{\delta_{\mathrm{cand}}}. (32)

Consequently, Condition 5.3 holds with

χ=2qcov,ncand=8qcov​log⁡2​|𝒢|​K​Tδcand.\chi=\frac{2}{q_{\mathrm{cov}}},\quad n_{\mathrm{cand}}=\frac{8}{q_{\mathrm{cov}}}\log\frac{2|\mathcal{G}|KT}{\delta_{\mathrm{cand}}}.

The proof is in Appendix C.4. Default smoothing gives qcov=pminq_{\mathrm{cov}}=p_{\min} and hence finite-horizon coverage, but pminp_{\min} decreases with TT: it does not establish the horizon-independent ratio used in the sharper OP summary. A horizon-independent lower bound on recommendation-aligned sampling instead gives constant χ\chi and logarithmic slack. Appendix A.7 illustrates nonempty design and count conditions, without asserting them for every adaptive OP trajectory. Table 5 summarizes the additional notation.

6 Numerical Experiments

This section gives finite-sample illustrations of the four mechanisms emphasized by the theory: robustness with a supplied corruption bound, adaptation when the corruption level is unknown, the distinct roles of reward and consumption corruption, and the pathwise resource-accounting guarantee. The experiments use the same clean population-LP benchmark as the analysis and evaluate reward with the clean conditional means, so corrupted feedback affects the learner but not the benchmark. We focus on robustness as the corruption level varies rather than fitting an empirical asymptotic exponent; the latter would mix finite-horizon initialization, master, design, and logarithmic terms that are kept explicit in Corollaries 4.2 and 5.3.

Algorithms and practical calibration. All headline policy comparisons use the on-policy mode from Sections 3.3 and 5. We use the norm-constrained Lasso implementation in Section 3.1 with fixed practical coefficients cρ=0.25c_{\rho}=0.25, cβ=0.75c_{\beta}=0.75, cC=1c_{C}=1, unit dual multiplier, start count 2020, and certified optimization gap 10−810^{-8}. Shared-Grid uses the complete dyadic grid, the explicit uniform-advice expert, the EXP4.P specification of Section 5, and 201201 safe cyclic initialization rounds (67 per non-null action). These settings are held fixed across the reported comparisons.

We compare ROPD with a valid supplied bound, a Reward-Only Robust ablation that protects reward confidence but not the consumption channel, and Non-Robust PD with zero corruption allowance. Shared-Grid receives no corruption bound. Attack maps are functions of the potential contexts and are fixed before the learner’s fresh action draw; compared methods receive the same contexts, clean potential outcomes, and exogenous attack map within each paired seed.

For a policy π\pi, define the reported percentage Relative Regret by

RelReg⁡(π):=100​VUB−∑t=1Tr0​(at,xt)VUB,\operatorname{RelReg}(\pi):=100\,\frac{V^{\mathrm{UB}}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}r^{0}(a_{t},x_{t})}{V^{\mathrm{UB}}}, (42)

where the null action contributes zero, including after stopping. Each reported cell uses 20 paired replications. Error bars and bands are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals from 2,000 whole-replication resamples; paired differences and corrupted-minus-clean increments are formed within seed before resampling, and rounds are never treated as independent replicates. The final runs used in this section have no excluded seeds, no clipping, and no solver failures.

6.2 Known corruption: performance as CZC_{Z} increases

We first study the setting of Theorem 4.1, where the learner is given a deterministic valid bound Γ≥CZ\Gamma\geq C_{Z}. Fix T=20,000T=20{,}000. Corruption targets Action 1 only on contexts where it is uniquely clean-preferred and applies the joint shift

(Δ​r1,Δ​b1,1,Δ​b1,2)=(−0.20,+0.10,+0.10).(\Delta r_{1},\Delta b_{1,1},\Delta b_{1,2})=(-0.20,+0.10,+0.10).

With Z=2Z=2, each attacked opportunity contributes 0.400.40 units to CZC_{Z}. We vary CZ∈{0,100,200,300,400}C_{Z}\in\{0,100,200,300,400\} by attacking 0,250,500,750,10000,250,500,750,1000 spread eligible opportunities.

Figure 1 reports absolute Relative Regret. All three methods coincide at CZ=0C_{Z}=0 (mean 0.756%0.756\%). ROPD has the lowest mean regret at every positive tested corruption level. At CZ=400C_{Z}=400, mean Relative Regret is 1.333%1.333\% for ROPD, 1.383%1.383\% for Reward-Only Robust, and 2.008%2.008\% for Non-Robust PD. Thus the separation from the non-robust baseline becomes substantial as corruption grows, while the Reward-Only ablation remains between the full robust method and the non-robust policy throughout the main sweep. This is consistent with the corruption-dependent terms in Corollary 4.2: the corruption-aware policies trade wider confidence sets for reduced sensitivity to contaminated feedback, and protecting both channels is useful when resource feedback can also be corrupted.

6.3 Unknown corruption: adaptation on one shared history

We next remove the corruption-bound input and evaluate Shared-Grid from Algorithm 2. Because Shared-Grid pays its initialization and master-comparison costs even on clean data, the primary quantity here is the corruption-induced increase

Δ​RelRegM⁡(CZ):=RelRegM⁡(CZ)−RelRegM⁡(0)\Delta\operatorname{RelReg}_{M}(C_{Z}):=\operatorname{RelReg}_{M}(C_{Z})-\operatorname{RelReg}_{M}(0) (43)

for method MM, formed within paired seeds. This isolates sensitivity to corruption from the method’s clean finite-horizon cost. Shared-Grid may still have larger absolute finite-horizon regret because it also pays initialization and master-comparison costs.

Fix T=80,000T=80{,}000 and vary the unknown corruption budget over CZ∈{0,1000,2000,3000,4000}C_{Z}\in\{0,1000,2000,3000,4000\}. The same joint shift (−0.20,+0.10,+0.10)(-0.20,+0.10,+0.10) targets clean-preferred Action 1 opportunities; Shared-Grid is never given CZC_{Z}. Figure 2 shows that Shared-Grid incurs a smaller corruption-induced increase at every positive severity. At CZ=4000C_{Z}=4000, the increase is 1.3131.313 percentage points for Shared-Grid versus 2.5742.574 for Non-Robust PD. The paired Shared-minus-Non-Robust differences are −0.262-0.262, −0.770-0.770, −0.916-0.916, and −1.261-1.261 percentage points at CZ=1000,2000,3000,4000C_{Z}=1000,2000,3000,4000, respectively; each pointwise paired 95% interval lies below zero.

These results illustrate the role of the adaptive grid in Theorem 5.2: even without a supplied corruption level, the shared-data master is markedly less sensitive to increasing corruption on this instance. The result should be read together with the explicit master term in Corollary 5.3. In absolute terms Shared-Grid still pays a visible clean finite-horizon master cost; the experiment therefore supports adaptation to corruption rather than an absolute dominance claim over the non-robust policy.

6.4 Reward, consumption, and joint corruption

The preceding experiments vary the amount of corruption. We now fix its effective budget and vary where it enters the feedback. Set T=40,000T=40{,}000 and attack the same 1,200 clean-preferred Action 1 opportunities in every corrupted condition. The shifts are

Reward:(−0.20,0,0),Consumption:(0,+0.10,+0.10),Joint:(−0.10,+0.05,+0.05).\begin{array}[]{ll}\text{Reward:}&(-0.20,0,0),\\ \text{Consumption:}&(0,+0.10,+0.10),\\ \text{Joint:}&(-0.10,+0.05,+0.05).\end{array}

Each attacked opportunity contributes 0.200.20 to CZC_{Z}, so all three conditions have exactly CZ=240C_{Z}=240, with the same target, attacked contexts, count, and timing within a paired seed.

Figure 3 reports absolute Relative Regret under the corrupted environments. ROPD has the lowest mean regret in all three channels: 0.416%0.416\% under reward corruption, 0.907%0.907\% under consumption corruption, and 0.655%0.655\% under joint corruption. Reward-Only Robust attains 0.501%0.501\%, 0.989%0.989\%, and 0.738%0.738\%, respectively, while Non-Robust PD attains 0.617%0.617\%, 1.086%1.086\%, and 0.840%0.840\%. The ordering is consistent across the three equal-CZC_{Z} corrupted environments and illustrates why consumption corruption is a separate modeling issue: it changes not only a regression target but also the resource-price and budget-accounting path. ROPD has the lowest absolute finite-horizon Relative Regret in each tested channel; the matched-clean incremental comparison is reported separately below and is more nuanced.

6.5 Pathwise resource accounting under corrupted consumption

Finally, we isolate the resource-accounting statement of Proposition 2.1. This controlled stress test uses the same problem scale (K=3K=3, m=2m=2, d=20d=20, s=3s=3) and perturbs one frequently used action–resource pair by ±0.10\pm 0.10. The goal is not a policy ranking: it is to make the two pathwise effects of consumption corruption visible.

When consumption is over-reported, the observed ledger is depleted too quickly and the safety rule can stop allocation early. Across increasing severities, mean lost rounds rise from zero to 341341 at the largest tested perturbation. When consumption is under-reported, the observed ledger remains feasible while clean resource use can exceed the nominal budget. At the largest severity, mean clean resource-1 excess is 361.243361.243 and mean played consumption corruption is Cb=363.665C_{b}=363.665. More importantly, every trajectory satisfies

Violobs⁡(T)=0,Violcl⁡(T)≤Cb​(T)≤CZ/Z,\Viol_{\mathrm{obs}}(T)=0,\qquad\Viol_{\mathrm{cl}}(T)\leq C_{b}(T)\leq C_{Z}/Z, (44)

with no additional additive unit. Thus Figure 4 directly illustrates the distinction between observed feasibility and clean feasibility that motivates the resource component of the theory.

6.6 Additional checks and interpretation

The main experiments above measure finite-horizon performance under known corruption, unknown corruption, different feedback channels, and corrupted resource accounting. We report three additional checks to clarify the interpretation of these results.

Matched clean controls. For the known-corruption algorithms, supplying a positive bound Γ\Gamma changes the confidence widths even when the observed feedback is clean. We therefore also compare each corrupted run with a clean run using the same supplied bound. This separates the effect of corrupted feedback from the finite-sample effect of the corruption-aware confidence allowance.

For the sweep in Figure 1, both robust methods have smaller matched corruption increments than Non-Robust PD at the two largest tested levels, CZ=300C_{Z}=300 and 400400. At CZ=400C_{Z}=400, the increments are 1.1531.153 percentage points for ROPD, 1.1131.113 for Reward-Only Robust, and 1.2521.252 for Non-Robust PD. The difference between ROPD and Reward-Only is small in this matched comparison, so Figure 1 is interpreted primarily as an absolute finite-horizon performance comparison.

The same control helps interpret Figure 3. With clean feedback and the same supplied Γ=240\Gamma=240, Relative Regret is 0.353%0.353\% for ROPD and 0.434%0.434\% for Reward-Only Robust, compared with 0.546%0.546\% in the ordinary Γ=0\Gamma=0 clean setting. Table 7 reports the resulting channel-specific increments.

The matched-control comparison gives a more refined view of the channel effects. In the consumption and joint conditions, the three incremental regrets are numerically close; Non-Robust PD has slightly smaller increments than ROPD by 0.01400.0140 and 0.00800.0080 percentage points, respectively, in the paired comparisons. This does not conflict with the absolute comparison in Figure 3. The robust methods also have lower matched clean regret when supplied with Γ=240\Gamma=240, and under the corrupted environments themselves ROPD attains the lowest Relative Regret in all three channels. Thus, Figure 3 summarizes finite-horizon performance under corruption, while the matched controls isolate the additional effect of corrupted feedback relative to each method’s corresponding clean baseline.

Horizon and design checks. A separate frozen horizon experiment uses T∈{40,000,80,000,160,000}T\in\{40{,}000,80{,}000,160{,}000\} with corruption of order T2/3T^{2/3}. The corruption-induced increase for Shared-Grid decreases from 1.6121.612 to 0.9200.920 percentage points over these horizons, while the corresponding increase for Non-Robust PD decreases from 3.5303.530 to 1.8511.851. Clean and corrupted Relative Regret also decrease with TT. These results provide a finite-horizon consistency check for the sublinear behavior in Corollaries 4.2 and 5.3, rather than an empirical estimate of their asymptotic exponents.

The experiment also has nondegenerate action-specific designs: all three specialist actions have positive clean LP mass, and their population second moments on the true reward supports are strictly positive. For Shared-Grid, candidate recommendations become meaningfully different under corruption; at CZ=4000C_{Z}=4000, grid candidates disagree on about 61%61\% of active post-initialization rounds. These diagnostics confirm that the finite-sample experiment exercises the learning and adaptation mechanisms studied in the theory.

Summary. The experiments illustrate four distinct parts of the analysis. With a supplied corruption bound, ROPD has lower absolute Relative Regret than the compared baselines throughout the tested corruption sweep. Without such a bound, Shared-Grid incurs substantially less corruption-induced degradation than Non-Robust PD across the tested unknown-corruption levels, while retaining its finite-horizon master cost. Across reward, consumption, and joint corruption, ROPD has the lowest absolute Relative Regret in the tested corrupted environments; the matched-clean incremental comparisons are more nuanced and are interpreted separately above. Finally, the accounting experiment directly illustrates exact observed feasibility and the corruption-controlled clean resource bound.

7 Conclusion and Limitations

We develop corruption-robust contextual allocation methods that account for both contaminated predictions and errors in resource accounting, pricing, and stopping. ROPD uses a supplied corruption bound, while Shared-Grid adapts confidence radii on one realized history. Both preserve observed budgets pathwise and control clean resource violation by consumption corruption. The estimator interface separates these allocation guarantees from the choice of sparse fitting method. Forced exploration provides one coverage route; the sharper on-policy rates require informative realized designs, with the additional recommendation-coverage condition for Shared-Grid. Obtaining less conservative calibration and weaker trajectory conditions remains a direction for further work.

Lemma A.8 (Bounded sub-Gaussian design calibration)

Under Assumptions 2.1 and 3.2, the FE retained histories, including a safe context-independent cyclic initialization, satisfy (47) with (49), simultaneously for all obtained prefixes n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, with failure probability at most δcov/2\delta_{\mathrm{cov}}/2.

A.7 A Nonempty Bounded-Context Instance

Let x=(1,ϵ2,…,ϵd)/dx=(1,\epsilon_{2},\ldots,\epsilon_{d})/\sqrt{d}, where the ϵj\epsilon_{j} are independent Rademacher signs. Then ‖x‖2=1\|x\|_{2}=1 and 𝔼​x​x⊤=Id/d\mathbb{E}xx^{\top}=I_{d}/d. For compatible sparse means, take s0=ss_{0}=s and choose θ⋆=d​(c​e1+∑j=2sbj​ej)\theta^{\star}=\sqrt{d}(ce_{1}+\sum_{j=2}^{s}b_{j}e_{j}) with 0<c−∑|bj|≤c+∑|bj|<10<c-\sum|b_{j}|\leq c+\sum|b_{j}|<1 and d⁡(c2+∑bj2)≤R2d(c^{2}+\sum b_{j}^{2})\leq R^{2}. Such choices exist for every R>0R>0 by scaling c,bjc,b_{j} down together. This gives sparse parameters with bounded, potentially context-dependent reward and consumption means. In this normalized class curvature is 1/d1/d; the coefficient AA must retain that dependence.

For illustration, context-independent uniform non-null sampling and budgets Bi≥T+1B_{i}\geq T+1 prevent safety stopping and give the same design event on all action histories. Moreover, Narec,Γ​(t)≤t−1≤2​K​Na​(t)+c​K​log⁡(K​T/δ)N_{a}^{\mathrm{rec},\Gamma}(t)\leq t-1\leq 2KN_{a}(t)+cK\log(KT/\delta) for any recommendations.
